I'll write about something that has been occupying my thoughts lately: the quiet revolution happening in how we understand attention and the architecture of human experience in an age of relentless stimulation.

---

## The Architecture of Attention in an Age of Noise

There is a peculiar sensation that arrives unannounced, usually in the liminal hours between afternoon and evening, when the light turns golden and slants through windows at that specific angle that makes dust motes visible. It is the feeling of having been somewhere else entirely—having been, in fact, nowhere at all, distributed across thirty tabs and half-formed thoughts and the phantom vibration of a phone that did not actually buzz—and suddenly, jarringly, finding yourself *here*, in a body, in a room, with the weight of your own consciousness pressing down like a hand on your shoulder. This is the return from the diffuse state, the scattered state, the state we have normalized so thoroughly that we no longer recognize it as a departure from anything.

I want to think about attention not as a resource to be managed, a commodity to be optimized, but as a form of relationship. We speak of "paying" attention, and the metaphor is apt in ways we rarely examine. Payment implies exchange, implies debt, implies a finite reserve. But what if we considered attention instead as a form of dwelling, of inhabiting? To attend to something is to live within it for a time, to make it the architecture of your temporary world. The question then becomes not how we allocate our attention efficiently, but what kinds of dwellings we are building, what kinds of habitations we are practicing, and what happens to a self that never fully inhabits anywhere.

The modern condition of attention is often described as fragmented, and the metaphor of fragmentation suggests something that was once whole and has been broken. But I am not sure this is accurate. I think instead we have become *diffuse*—not broken but spread thin, stretched across networks and notifications and the constant low-grade hum of potential elsewhere. The self in this condition is not so much shattered as it is attenuated, present everywhere in thin traces and fully present nowhere. We have invented a new form of being, distributed consciousness, and we are only beginning to understand its costs.

Consider the experience of reading a book, which has become, for many, almost an archaeological practice. Not the reading of screens, with their hyperlinks and their infinite scroll, but the reading of pages that do not update, that contain only what they contain, that ask you to proceed sequentially through a structure someone else has built and that you cannot alter. There is a strange passivity to this, a submission to another's architecture, that feels almost transgressive now. To read a book is to agree to be led, to follow a path without checking maps, to encounter ideas without the possibility of immediate verification or refutation or distraction. You cannot, mid-sentence, look up what else the author has said, or what their critics have said, or what unrelated thing has happened in the world in the last four minutes. You are simply *there*, in the text, with only your own thoughts for company.

This solitude of reading used to be ordinary. Now it requires intention, protection, almost a kind of defiance. The spaces that once made it easy—the quiet room, the unscheduled afternoon, the walk without destination—have become endangered habitats. We have filled them with podcasts and playlists and the constant possibility of connection, as if solitude were a problem to be solved rather than a condition to be inhabited. And in doing so, we have perhaps lost something about how thinking happens, how it requires the friction of slowness, the productive boredom of being stuck with only yourself.

But I do not want to romanticize a past that was never as still as we imagine. The pre-digital world had its own noise, its own distractions, its own forms of diffusion. What is different now is the *intentionality* of the attention economy, the systematic, data-driven, A/B-tested optimization of platforms for engagement, which is to say for the capture and holding of attention by any means available. This is not merely noise; it is noise designed to be maximally effective, to exploit the particular vulnerabilities of human psychology, to create loops of intermittent reinforcement that keep us returning, scrolling, checking, not because we choose to but because the architecture has been engineered to make choosing otherwise difficult.

The philosopher Byung-Chul Han writes about the "burnout society," the achievement society, where we are no longer exploited by external oppressors but exploit ourselves, driven by internalized imperatives to optimize, to produce, to be constantly available. I think there is something to this, but I also think it misses the extent to which these internalized imperatives are not merely cultural but *structural*, built into the very interfaces through which we conduct our lives. The notification is not a neutral tool; it is a demand encoded in software, a tiny act of violence against your present attention, a claim that something else matters more than where you are now. And the accumulation of these tiny violences, hundreds or thousands per day, creates a kind of ambient trauma, a constant low-level emergency that keeps us in a state of reactive vigilance, never fully at rest, never fully anywhere.

What would it mean to resist this, not through grand gestures of digital detox or retreat to monastic spaces, but through the cultivation of different habits of attention, different architectures of daily life? I think of the writer Jenny Odell's practice of "doing nothing," which is not really doing nothing but doing things that resist the logic of productivity and optimization—birdwatching, looking at plants, wandering without destination. These activities are radical not because they are natural or authentic but because they are *unharvestable*, they do not generate data, they do not contribute to profiles, they cannot be efficiently monetized. They exist in a different economy entirely.

Or I think of the musician and writer Brian Eno's concept of "ambient" music, designed to be "as ignorable as it is interesting," to create a space rather than demand focus. This is attention as environment, as atmosphere, something you inhabit rather than expend. The contrast with the playlist designed for productivity, the binaural beats for focus, the endless optimization of the sonic environment for maximum output, is instructive. One model treats attention as something to be husbanded and directed; the other treats it as something to be surrounded, to be given room to move and settle where it will.

I have been trying, imperfectly, to notice what happens to my thinking in different conditions of attention. The thinking that happens while walking, without phone, without destination, has a different quality than the thinking that happens at a desk with a screen. It is slower, more associative, more apt to make unexpected connections. It is also more apt to become uncomfortable, to encounter thoughts I would prefer to avoid, to feel the weight of problems I have been too busy to acknowledge. The screen offers a constant escape from this discomfort, a way to keep moving, to keep consuming, to never fully arrive at anything difficult. The walk offers no such escape, and this is precisely its value.

There is a kind of attention that develops in conditions of slowness and limitation that I want to call *thickness*—the opposite of the thin, distributed attention of the scroll. Thick attention is when you are really seeing something, when the thing reveals itself in its particularity, its resistance to your categories, its stubborn existence beyond your use of it. The tree that is not "a tree" but this specific arrangement of bark and branch and the particular quality of light filtering through leaves that will never be exactly this way again. The conversation that is not an exchange of information but a mutual unfolding, where you are listening not to respond but to understand, to be changed by what you hear. The work that is not a task to be completed but a practice to be entered, where the process matters more than the product, where you are willing to be inefficient, to take wrong turns, to dwell in uncertainty.

This thickness of attention is, I suspect, where meaning accumulates. Not the meaning of grand narratives or ultimate purposes, but the local, specific meaning of having been present for something, of having let it matter to you, of having built a relationship with it over time. The thin attention of the feed gives us breadth without depth, variety without development, connection without intimacy. We know many things shallowly and nothing well. We have many acquaintances and few friends. We have experienced much and been changed by little.

I am interested in the practices, small and large, that might cultivate thickness. The obvious ones—meditation, contemplative prayer, sustained artistic practice—have been discussed extensively. But I am also interested in the mundane architectures of attention: how we arrange our spaces, how we schedule our time, how we relate to our devices. The practice of leaving the phone in another room. The practice of not checking email until a certain hour. The practice of doing one thing at a time, however inefficient this seems. These are not moral disciplines but *attentional* disciplines, ways of shaping the conditions under which consciousness unfolds.

There is something here about the relationship between attention and memory, too. We do not remember what we do not fully attend to; the diffuse self leaves diffuse traces. The days blur, the weeks become indistinguishable, time seems to accelerate as we age not because time actually speeds up but because we are paying less attention, because experience is becoming thinner, less memorable, less *lived*. The paradox of the optimized life is that it produces so little that is worth remembering, so little that is distinct enough to stand out from the continuous flow. We are busy making memories we will never have.

I think sometimes about the last generations that lived without photography, without the ability to capture and preserve images of their experience. They had to remember differently, to build their memories through attention and repetition and narrative, to make the important things memorable by the quality of their engagement with them. We have outsourced much of this work to our devices, and in doing so, we have perhaps also outsourced some of the depth of our engagement. The photograph is a promise that we will not have to remember, that the moment can be preserved without being fully inhabited. And so we photograph constantly, building archives of thinly experienced moments, and we remember less and less of what we have so thoroughly documented.

What would it mean to attend to attention itself, to make the quality of our awareness an object of concern? This is the project of contemplative traditions across cultures, and it is also, I think, a necessary project for anyone living in the contemporary world. Not to achieve some ideal state of pure focus, which is probably impossible and possibly undesirable, but to become more *aware* of how our attention is being shaped, where it is going, what it is being spent on. To notice the pull of the notification, the itch of the check, the relief of distraction. To understand these as phenomena, as experiences that happen in a body and a mind and a particular social context, rather than as inevitable responses to the nature of things.

There is a kind of freedom that emerges from this awareness, even if the external conditions do not change. The freedom to choose, sometimes, to attend differently. To close the tab, to turn off the sound, to let the message wait. To build, in small ways, spaces and times where attention can thicken, where the self can gather itself and become present. This is not a solution to the attention economy, which is a structural problem requiring structural responses. But it is a practice of resistance, a way of maintaining some territory that is not fully colonized, some capacity for dwelling that is not fully monetized.

I am writing this on a computer, connected to the internet, with the possibility of distraction always present. I have checked my email twice in the writing, have been pulled by the notification of a message I did not need to see. The attention economy is not something outside me that I can simply oppose; it is something I inhabit, that shapes my habits and desires, that I am complicit in even when I critique it. This is the difficulty of the problem: we are not innocent victims but active participants, and the transformation we need is not just of systems but of selves, of the very ways we have learned to want and to be.

And yet, and yet. The afternoon light is changing, becoming more horizontal, more golden. I have been writing for some time now, and there have been moments—this is one of them—when the writing has carried me somewhere beyond the immediate conditions of its production, when I have been, for stretches of minutes, fully in it, not checking, not wandering, just here, making sentences, following thoughts where they lead. This is not the thickness of a lifetime's practice, but it is something, a glimpse of what attention can do when it gathers, when it is allowed to dwell. The possibility of such moments is what makes the effort worthwhile, what makes the resistance meaningful.

I want to end not with a conclusion but with an image, a practice of attention I have been trying to cultivate. It is the practice of looking at one thing for longer than is comfortable. Not analyzing it, not photographing it, not using it for anything, just looking, letting the initial impressions settle, letting the mind move through its predictable categories, and then continuing to look, past the point of boredom, past the point of restlessness, into something else that opens when the demand for novelty and utility is refused. What emerges is rarely spectacular. It is usually quiet, specific, resistant to generalization. But it is real, and it is mine, and it has not been harvested or optimized or turned into content. It is simply an experience of having been present, of having built, however briefly, a thicker habitation.

The world will not slow down. The notifications will not stop. The attention economy will continue to expand, to find new frontiers, to monetize new forms of awareness. But within this, there remains the possibility of different practices, different architectures, different ways of being with ourselves and with the world. The question is not how to escape the noise but how to find, within it and against it, spaces of quiet dwelling. The question is not how to optimize attention but how to make it more fully human, more capable of the thickness that gives experience its weight and meaning. This is work that is never finished, that must be taken up again each day, that offers no final victory but only the ongoing practice of presence. And in a world that is constantly pulling us elsewhere, this practice of presence is, perhaps, the most radical thing we can do.
